content.title: 3. RISK CALCULATORS
content.narrative_summary: The page introduces the role of cardiovascular risk indices in preoperative assessment, noting that multivariable-derived scores (eg, RCRI, NSQIP perioperative MI and cardiac arrest risk calculators) have been validated but show variability in predicted risk and inconsistent endpoints. Emerging approaches combining traditional scores with imaging (eg, coronary calcium via CT) may enhance stratification, although discrimination is poorer in vascular surgery. The recommendation-specific text describes commonly used tools: ASA Physical Status classification, RCRI (with modest discrimination, defining low-risk as estimated MACE <1%), the universal NSQIP risk calculator (30-day mortality estimation), and the AUB-HAS2 cardiovascular risk index (stratifying 30-day event risk into low/intermediate/high categories). A simplified 3-factor method for low MI incidence is also noted.

content.title: 3.2. Functional Capacity Assessment
content.narrative_summary: Functional capacity is an important predictor of adverse cardiovascular events after noncardiac surgery and is commonly measured in METs, with <4 METs indicating poor capacity. It can be assessed by patient-reported ability to climb stairs or via instruments such as the Duke Activity Status Index (DASI). In selected cases, exercise stress testing provides an objective assessment, but most asymptomatic patients proceed without further testing. Poor functional capacity is associated with increased risk of perioperative cardiac events, and structured assessment can guide preoperative risk stratification. Supportive studies include a 600-patient study showing a 2-fold increased risk in patients unable to walk 4 blocks or climb 2 flights of stairs, the BASEL-PMI study demonstrating higher rates of death or MI in those with <2 flights capacity, and large cohort analyses confirming added predictive value of functional capacity measures.

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients undergoing elevated-risk NCS, a structured assessment of functional capacity (such as the Duke Activity Status Index [DASI]) is reasonable to stratify the risk of perioperative adverse cardiovascular events.1-8

content.title: 3.3. Frailty
content.narrative_summary: Older patients undergoing noncardiac surgery (NCS) are at increased risk for cardiac and noncardiac complications due to frailty, a syndrome of physiological decline across organ systems. Frailty prevalence rises with age, is higher in women and in those with heart failure, and is associated with increased mortality, complications, length of stay, and functional decline. Prehabilitation (physical conditioning and nutritional support) before surgery may improve outcomes. A meta-analysis of studies linked frailty with elevated 30-day mortality and complication rates, and multiple validated screening instruments for frailty are available.

rows.recommendation: In all patients ≥65 years of age and in those <64 years with perceived frailty who are undergoing elevated-risk NCS, preoperative frailty assessment using a validated tool can be useful for evaluating perioperative risk and guiding management.¹⁻⁵

content.title: 4.2 Assessment of Ventricular Function
content.narrative_summary: Synopsis: Abnormal left ventricular (LV) systolic or diastolic function is associated with increased perioperative major adverse cardiac events (MACE) in noncardiac surgery, with risk higher in patients with lower LV ejection fraction (LVEF), higher-risk procedures, and additional comorbid factors. Large cohort studies (Medicare beneficiaries, U.S. Veterans Affairs) report increased 30- and 90-day mortality and readmissions in patients with symptomatic or asymptomatic heart failure (HF) regardless of LVEF, and grade 3 diastolic dysfunction confers higher MACE risk than grades 1–2. Assessment of LV function is indicated for unexplained cardiac symptoms or elevated preoperative BNP/NT-proBNP, whereas routine evaluation in stable, asymptomatic patients lacks supporting evidence. Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text: HF is an established risk factor for poor perioperative outcomes; in a cohort of 159,237 noncardiac surgery patients, 18% had HF and 34% had CAD, with significantly higher mortality and HF readmissions in HF versus CAD; smaller studies evaluating preoperative ECG, hemoglobin testing, and focused cardiac ultrasound are ongoing.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Assessment of Left Ventricular Function. Referenced studies that support the recommendations are summarized in the Online Data Supplement.

rows.recommendation: In patients undergoing NCS with new dyspnea, physical examination findings of HF, or suspected new/worsening ventricular dysfunction, it is recommended to perform preoperative evaluation of LV function to help guide perioperative management.

In patients with a known diagnosis of HF with worsening dyspnea or other change in clinical status undergoing NCS, preoperative assessment of LV function is reasonable to help guide perioperative management.
In asymptomatic and clinically stable patients undergoing NCS, routine preoperative evaluation of LV function is not recommended due to lack of benefit.

3. In patients with non-left main CAD who are planned for NCS, routine preoperative coronary revascularization is not recommended to reduce perioperative cardiovascular events.

section_headings: 6.2 Hypertension and Perioperative Blood Pressure Management
content.narrative_summary: The page begins by continuing discussion of preoperative coronary revascularization trials (including CARP) in patients with significant left main CAD, noting no mortality benefit and higher bleeding complications with PCI, especially after drug-eluting stents, and a meta-analysis of 3,949 patients showing no routine revascularization benefit before noncardiac surgery. It then presents the impact of perioperative blood pressure: uncontrolled hypertension affects ~25% of patients undergoing major noncardiac surgery, increasing myocardial demand and risk of cardiovascular, cerebrovascular, and bleeding events; intraoperative and postoperative hypotension similarly raises adverse cardiovascular and renal risks; high-quality RCTs are limited, acute lowering of perioperative BP may not reduce and could harm, and BP assessment should consider systolic, diastolic, mean, or pulse pressure metrics.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Hypertension and Perioperative Blood Pressure Management

rows.recommendation: In most* patients with hypertension planned for elective NCS, it is reasonable to continue medical therapy for hypertension throughout the perioperative period.†

In patients undergoing elective elevated-risk surgery who have cardiovascular risk factors for perioperative complications‡ and recent history of poorly controlled hypertension (systolic blood pressure [SBP] ≥180 mm Hg or diastolic blood pressure [DBP] ≥110 mm Hg before the day of surgery), deferring surgery may be considered to reduce the risk of perioperative complications.† 1-2
In patients undergoing NCS, maintaining an intraoperative mean arterial pressure (MAP) ≥60 to 65 mm Hg or SBP ≥90 mm Hg is recommended to reduce the risk of myocardial injury.3-9

In patients undergoing NCS, treatment of hypotension (MAP <60-65 or SBP <90 mm Hg) in the postoperative period is recommended to limit the risk of cardiovascular, cerebrovascular, renal events, and mortality.6

In patients with hypertension undergoing NCS, it is recommended that preoperative antihypertensive medications be restarted as soon as clinically reasonable to avoid complications from postoperative hypertension.

content.narrative_summary: Patients with heart failure (HF) face increased perioperative risk, including higher 30- and 90-day mortality, especially with reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF). HF history is incorporated into standard preoperative risk indices (RCRI, NSQIP). Guideline-directed medical therapies (GDMT) reduce risk, but interruption without indication increases mortality. SGLT2 inhibitors are linked to perioperative metabolic acidosis and should be withheld before surgery. In advanced or decompensated HF, consider postponing elective surgery and obtaining cardiology consultation.

rows.recommendation: In patients with HF undergoing elective NCS, sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) should be withheld for 3 to 4 days* before surgery when feasible to reduce the risk of perioperative metabolic acidosis.
rows.supporting_text: *Canagliflozin, dapagliflozin, and empagliflozin should be stopped ≥3 days and ertugliflozin ≥4 days before scheduled surgery.

rows.recommendation: In patients with compensated HF undergoing NCS, it is reasonable to continue GDMT (excluding SGLT2i) in the perioperative period, unless contraindicated, to reduce the risk of worsening HF.

content.title: Synopsis
content.narrative_summary: This page provides a synopsis of perioperative management for patients with severe aortic stenosis (AS) undergoing noncardiac surgery (NCS), highlighting the increased risk associated with low-flow, low-gradient AS, the importance of multidisciplinary heart valve team involvement (Figure 2), and the role of echocardiography within one year of elevated‐risk NCS. It discusses consideration of transcatheter or surgical aortic valve replacement (AVR) or balloon aortic valvuloplasty in selected patients to reduce perioperative risk. The Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text summarizes available data on outcomes of AVR performed immediately before NCS, including reduced MACE and mortality in treated versus untreated severe AS, limited series on valvuloplasty, and recommendations for perioperative monitoring (invasive hemodynamics, intraoperative TEE) and multidisciplinary consultation.

figures_tables_algorithms.title: Management of Patients With Severe Aortic Stenosis Requiring Elective or Time-Sensitive Noncardiac Surgery
figures_tables_algorithms.summary: Flowchart guiding management of patients with severe aortic stenosis (AS) requiring elective or time-sensitive noncardiac surgery (NCS). All patients undergo multidisciplinary team discussions (cardiology, anesthesiology, surgery). Symptomatic severe AS patients are evaluated for aortic valve replacement (AVR) before elevated-risk NCS, with team-based, patient-centered decision for transcatheter (TAVI) versus surgical AVR (SAVR). Asymptomatic severe AS is stratified by left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF): for LVEF <50%, assess if NCS can be delayed; if yes, team-based decision on how to proceed; if no, proceed with AVR evaluation as above. For LVEF ≥50%, if surgery is elevated-risk, AVR evaluation; if low-risk, reasonable to proceed with elective low-risk NCS.

content.title: 6.4.2. Mitral Stenosis
content.narrative_summary: Patients with moderate to severe mitral stenosis (MS) are at increased risk of perioperative adverse cardiovascular events and should be evaluated by echocardiography and managed by a multidisciplinary team. Patients meeting criteria for valve intervention (symptomatic NYHA ≥II or asymptomatic with elevated pulmonary pressures or new atrial fibrillation) should undergo mitral valve (MV) intervention before elective noncardiac surgery (NCS) when feasible. If MV intervention cannot be performed preoperatively, perioperative goals include maintaining a low-normal heart rate, adequate preload and vascular resistance, and rhythm control; intensive or invasive hemodynamic monitoring may facilitate early detection and management of tachycardia, hypotension, pulmonary edema, and other complications.

rows.recommendation: 1. Patients with severe mitral stenosis (MS) should be evaluated for the need for mitral valve (MV) intervention before elective NCS.1-17

2. In patients with severe MS who cannot undergo MV intervention before NCS, perioperative invasive hemodynamic monitoring is reasonable to guide management to reduce the risk of cardiovascular complications.

3. In patients with severe MS who cannot undergo MV intervention before NCS, perioperative heart-rate control (eg, beta blockers, calcium channel blockers [CCBs], ivabradine, digoxin) may be considered to prolong diastolic filling time and decrease perioperative cardiovascular complications.18-21

content.narrative_summary: This section outlines supportive evidence for the management of new-onset postoperative atrial fibrillation (POAF) after noncardiac surgery (NCS). content.narrative_summary: Calcium channel blockers (CCBs) include nondihydropyridine agents (verapamil, diltiazem) and dihydropyridine agents (amlodipine, felodipine, nifedipine extended release). Dihydropyridines are primarily used for hypertension management, while nondihydropyridines treat cardiac dysrhythmias and relieve angina. Perioperative CCB administration has been examined in small RCTs. A 2003 meta-analysis of 11 RCTs (1007 patients) comparing perioperative CCBs versus placebo found no reduction in mortality or perioperative MI but did find reductions in composite MI and death and postoperative supraventricular tachycardia; individual studies showed hypotension and bradycardia. A more recent meta-analysis of dihydropyridines versus other antihypertensives in 14 studies noted no significant differences in postoperative hemodynamics. Current data do not support initiating CCBs perioperatively, although continuation may be reasonable with awareness of potential intraoperative hypotension (dihydropyridines) and bradycardia (nondihydropyridines).

section_headings: 7.5 Antiplatelet Therapy and Timing of Noncardiac Surgery in Patients With Coronary Artery Disease
content.narrative_summary: The page includes a synopsis stating that a large randomized controlled trial (POISE-2) showed no benefit of initiating clonidine to prevent perioperative MACE and raised safety concerns, so initiation is not recommended. Chronic perioperative continuation of alpha-2 agonists remains unstudied, and their use is reserved for patients with severe resistant hypertension. The Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text summarizes the blinded POISE-2 trial of 10,010 noncardiac surgery patients randomized to low-dose clonidine versus placebo, finding no reduction in 30-day death or nonfatal MI but significantly increased bradycardia and hypotension, with additional RCTs and meta-analyses corroborating these safety concerns.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Antiplatelet Therapy and Timing of Noncardiac Surgery in Patients With Coronary Artery Disease

rows.recommendation: For patients with CAD undergoing elective NCS, management of perioperative antiplatelet therapy and timing of surgery should be determined by a multidisciplinary team with shared decision-making to weigh the risks of bleeding, thrombosis, and consequences of delayed surgery.
In patients with recent coronary artery balloon angioplasty without stent placement, elective NCS should be delayed for a minimum of 14 days to minimize perioperative MACE.
In patients with DES-PCI placed for ACS who require elective NCS with interruption of ≥1 antiplatelet agents, surgery should ideally be delayed ≥12 months to minimize perioperative MACE.
In patients with DES-PCI placed for CCD who require elective NCS with interruption of ≥1 antiplatelet agents, it is reasonable to delay surgery for ≥6 months after PCI to minimize perioperative MACE.

In patients with DES-PCI who require time-sensitive NCS with interruption of ≥1 antiplatelet agents, NCS may be considered ≥3 months after PCI if the risk of delaying surgery outweighs the risk of MACE.

In patients with a recent (≤30 days) bare-metal stent (BMS) or DES-PCI, elective NCS requiring interruption of ≥1 antiplatelet agents is potentially harmful due to a high risk of stent thrombosis and ischemic complications.
In patients with prior PCI undergoing NCS, it is recommended to continue aspirin* (75-100 mg), if possible, to reduce the risk of cardiac events.

In patients with CAD who require time-sensitive NCS within 30 days of PCI with BMS or <3 months of PCI with DES, DAPT should be continued unless the risk of bleeding outweighs the benefit of the prevention of stent thrombosis.

section_headings: Perioperative Antiplatelet Management in Patients Without Prior PCI
content.narrative_summary: The Synopsis highlights the complex balance between thrombotic and bleeding risks when interrupting antiplatelet therapy for noncardiac surgery in patients with coronary artery disease and prior PCI. It notes that stent thrombosis risk peaks 1–6 weeks post-PCI and persists to 6 months, recommends six months of DAPT followed by monotherapy, and mentions selected shorter DAPT durations and the need for further study in urgent cases. The Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text emphasizes a multidisciplinary approach involving the patient, surgeon, anesthesiologist, and cardiologist to individualize timing of antiplatelet interruption and continuation, acknowledges limited data for balloon angioplasty without stent and for patients with prior DES-PCI, and underscores careful risk balancing.

rows.recommendation: In patients with prior PCI in whom OAC monotherapy must be discontinued before NCS, aspirin should be substituted when feasible in the perioperative period until OAC can be safely reinitiated.

In select patients after PCI who have a high thrombotic risk, perioperative bridging with intravenous antiplatelet therapy may be considered <6 months after DES or <30 days after BMS if NCS cannot be deferred.
In patients with CCD without prior PCI undergoing elective NCS, it may be reasonable to continue aspirin in selected patients when the risk of cardiac events outweighs the risk of bleeding.
In patients with CAD but without prior PCI who are undergoing elective noncardiac NCS, routine initiation of aspirin is not beneficial.

content.title: 7.6. Oral Anticoagulants
content.narrative_summary: The page begins by concluding that perioperative aspirin did not reduce death or MI but did increase major bleeding, and that chronic aspirin withdrawal in vascular surgery patients was not linked to increased cardiovascular events. content.narrative_summary: This section reviews observational evidence on perioperative management of oral anticoagulants (OACs), including delaying noncardiac surgery in high residual thrombotic risk, and the preference for time-based reversal of OACs where feasible. Measurement of coagulation parameters or drug levels can identify ongoing drug effects; absence of altered parameters may obviate reversal. Rapid reversal strategies include prothrombin complex concentrates and andexanet alfa for factor Xa inhibitors (rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban) or idarucizumab for dabigatran. High-bleeding–risk procedures should involve complete interruption of OACs, holding anticoagulants for ≥5 half-lives (≥3 days for factor Xa inhibitors, ≥4 days for dabigatran if creatinine clearance <50 mL/min). In high-thrombotic–risk patients on vitamin K antagonists, perioperative bridging with parenteral anticoagulation is common but lacks efficacy/safety data; meta-analyses and the PERIOP-2 randomized trial suggest bridging increases bleeding without clear reduction in thromboembolism. content.title: 8.2. Perioperative Pain Management
content.narrative_summary: Pain is common after surgery and can trigger tachyarrhythmias and hypertension, increasing myocardial oxygen demand and risk of type 2 MI in patients with CAD. Intravenous or regional analgesia, particularly epidural techniques (TEA for abdominal surgery, lumbar epidural for hip and lower extremity fractures), provides acute postoperative pain relief. TEA has been shown in RCTs and large database analyses to reduce postoperative MI, tachyarrhythmias, and cardiopulmonary complications compared with intravenous opioid‐based management. Enhanced recovery protocols increasingly incorporate TEA. Adjunctive agents (gabapentin, pregabalin) have had limited opioid‐sparing success and carry risks of visual disturbances, dizziness, and respiratory depression in older patients.

rows.recommendation: For patients undergoing major abdominal surgery, the use of epidural analgesia for postoperative pain relief is reasonable to decrease the incidence of perioperative cardiac events.
For patients with a hip fracture waiting for surgical repair, epidural analgesia may be considered to decrease the incidence of preoperative cardiac events.

content.title: 2024 Perioperative Cardiovascular Management for Noncardiac Surgery Guideline
content.narrative_summary: Synopsis: Perioperative myocardial injury occurs in approximately 20% of patients undergoing noncardiac surgery (NCS). It spans a spectrum from asymptomatic myocardial injury to overt postoperative myocardial infarction, defined by ischemic symptoms, ECG changes, pathologic Q-waves, or imaging evidence of myocardial loss. Myocardial injury after noncardiac surgery (MINS) includes both type 1 and type 2 MI, often without symptoms due to anesthesia or analgesia. Diagnosis requires more than one elevated cardiac troponin (cTn) above the 99th percentile excluding nonischemic causes, and is associated with adverse short- and long-term outcomes, including a 30-day mortality of approximately 10% and population‐attributable risk of 34%. Predictors include cardiovascular risk factors, kidney disease, and urgent surgery. Underlying etiology is presumed atherosclerotic coronary artery disease. Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text: 1) Troponin surveillance may be reasonable in patients with known cardiovascular disease or high-risk surgery, as elevated postoperative cTn correlates with a 3- to 5-fold increase in 30-day mortality. 2) In low-risk populations, routine troponin surveillance is unlikely to identify injury or confer benefit. 3) Elevated postoperative cTn identifies patients at increased risk for adverse events; observational data suggest early cardiology consultation, antiplatelet and statin therapy, and intensification of medical therapy may reduce mortality. 4) Postoperative administration of direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) may decrease long-term cardiovascular event risk [text continues].

section_headings: 10.1. Preoperative Evaluation Before Liver and Kidney Transplantation
content.narrative_summary: Synopsis paragraphs describe the higher cardiovascular risk and targeted preoperative CAD screening strategies for patients undergoing liver and kidney transplantation; outcomes and perioperative cardiovascular considerations in patients with obesity undergoing bariatric surgery; and the introduction to cost–value assessments for medical therapies.

rows.recommendation: Patients with perioperative NSTEMI should receive GDMT as recommended for nonsurgical patients with spontaneous MI. In some cases, GDMT may need to be tailored based on hemodynamic status and bleeding risks. Medical therapy should include at least 1 antiplatelet, provided the benefits outweigh the bleeding risks, and initiation of a high-intensity statin. In patients whose hemodynamic status permits, beta blockers, ACEi, and nitrates may be considered for both symptomatic relief from angina and long-term cardiovascular risk reduction.

ICA may be appropriate in selected perioperative patients with postoperative NSTEMI. In retrospective observational analyses, invasive management of MI was associated with lower in-hospital mortality compared with conservative management. However, given the potential need for systemic anticoagulation and longer-term antiplatelet therapies after PCI, the decision to pursue invasive treatment should be balanced with the risk of residual postoperative bleeding, type of surgery, and time since surgery. The severity of clinical presentation, peak cTn concentration, presence of ischemic electrocardiographic changes, and other patient-specific factors should also be considered. Individuals with ongoing symptoms not responsive to GDMT, evidence of hemodynamic instability, persistent biomarker elevation, or imaging evidence of new regional wall motion abnormalities or reduced ventricular function may derive the greatest benefit from urgent ICA in the perioperative period. Decisions to pursue invasive management of MI after NCS should be undertaken in a team-based manner, involving the surgeon, anesthesiologist, and cardiologist.

12. Evidence Gaps and Future Research Directions
content.narrative_summary: This section reviews cost and diagnostic performance of stress testing modalities in stable patients undergoing noncardiac surgery (NCS). Stress echocardiography demonstrates higher accuracy and fewer inconclusive results than exercise ECG, is associated with fewer downstream invasive procedures and clinic visits, and yields cost savings in low-risk patients when using deferral tools. Findings from the PROMISE trial, including functional flow reserve–guided CCTA, provide insights but should not be extrapolated directly to preoperative evaluation due to different patient cohorts. Section 12 outlines evidence gaps and future research priorities: the need for rigorous multidisciplinary perioperative care delivery and telemedicine studies; validation of perioperative risk indices; high-quality RCTs on blood pressure thresholds, AF rate vs rhythm control, and revascularization strategies; optimal timing of surgery after LVAD implant or recent stroke; and the lack of demonstrated benefit of stress testing or catheterization without troponin elevation.
